newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romanians lose state insurance, have little else.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romanians lose state insurance, have little else.

text.p: Beware of fire, flood and ill fortune in Romania, says the best local advice. Most probably you will not be insured against calamity.
Romania is slowly dismantling its state insurance monopoly but it has built little by way of a commercial safety net for individuals and companies walking the tightrope of risk.
Under pressure to open up the financial industry to outsiders, the government has scrapped communist-era mandatory insurance cover for property and vehicle passengers.
Car owners must choose third-party insurance themselves from October and state property cover mostly expires next year.

That has cleared the way for more foreign competition and an explosion in the domestic insurance industry -- but so far interest has been slight, leaving former state monopoly holders to prospect for most of the market.

"The market has great potential but is not exploited enough," said Emil Boldus, president of the National Union of Insurance and Reinsurance Companies (UNSAR). "We need the financial strength and knowledge of big foreign companies."

Business should boom in a country with 23 million people, rising car ownership and the continuing privatisation, albeit sluggish, of thousands of state companies. But without the appropriate legal architecture, growth is forecast as small.

More than 40 insurers have opened over the past six years, but few are solid enough to stand up to state-owned ASIROM, which controls more than half the business and held the monopoly on compulsory insurance.
The overall insurance market remains thin, taking only some 0.4 percent of gross domestic product. Theft, pension, crop and health insurance are almost entirely unavailable.
With minimum equity requirements unchanged since 1991, the total capital of insurers operating in Romania was only 77 billion lei ($23.87 million) at the end of 1995.
"The present capital requirement is ridiculous. There are plenty of players on the market but most of them are undercapitalised," said Boldus.

Anyone with around $8,000 in his pocket can set up an insurer in Romania, said Boldus, adding that less than a third of local insurance companies had the 1.0 billion lei in capital that would take them close to minimum western standards.
"There are some 160 so-called brokers but I doubt more than 10 are what an insurance broker is supposed to be," he said.
The insurance supervisory body OSAR acknowledges the need to raise present capital requirements by at least 10 times but says the move has to be stipulated by a new law.
"The insurance market will then crystallise, we will see mergers and switches of activity. Only 10 or 15 companies will be left, but they will be solid," said Nicolae Crisan, head of OSAR.

With companies aware of the scope for growth, competition is fierce, with some firms slashing premiums below profitable levels, compromising financial safety and risking the scandals that have dogged other parts of the country's finance industry.
Total premium incomes almost doubled to 290 billion lei last year from 164 billion in 1994, while profits of insurance companies rose to 51 billion lei from 48 billion.

"Most insurers just want more premiums and that's why they are low. Insurers don't really care whether they can cover the risks they take," said Valentin Tuca, manager of Marsh & McLennan's local branch.

Analysts say few insurers put their gains into reserves and a lack of capital strength has forced most companies to seek reinsurance abroad, using up the bulk of collected premiums -- especially from aviation and maritime policies.
Aviation insurance premium incomes tripled to 9.6 billion lei last year but some 85 percent flew abroad for reinsurance.
In a bid to reduce premium outflow the law asks Romanian insurers to seek cover among local players. Only if three refuse can insurers then resort to international markets.
"What we need in this market is a (local) reinsurer," said Crisan.
Some big international insurers have dipped their toes in the Romanian market.

Italy's Assicurazioni Generali Spa and American International Group Inc operate joint ventures and market sources say ING Group, which has businesses across central Europe, will soon enter the life insurance field.
Income from life insurance rose to 31.5 billion lei last year, 67 percent up in real terms from 1994, but such policies take up only 11 percent of the market.

Some analysts say major foreign involvement will only follow the privatisation of state giants ASIROM and ASTRA, underwriter of hard currency policies, but the sale of such precious state assets will be a long time coming.
Tougher supervision and a greater awareness of the need for insurance are also essential if the market is to take off.
"This market hasn't had to cope with big problems so far as the private sector is still underdeveloped and major industrial risks still go uninsured," said Tuca.
Industry experts say the insurance law should be amended to give the OSAR the right to influence premiums and to counter potential dumping practices by large companies.
Analysts say most state company managers have failed to grasp the importance of insurance.
"No one has made them take such policies in the past. And their managers now bear no responsibility in case of accidents if they haven't thought to cover the risks," one source said. ($1=3226 Lei)
